articles.title: ICE is hiding detainees from their families – and the death toll is rising
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content: ICE just scrubbed tens of thousands of people from its Online Detainee Locator System, leaving their families and legal teams in the dark. Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, senior fellow at the American Immigration Council, joins Zoe Alexandra and Rania Khalek to break down how DHS effectively “disappeared” at least 20,000 people with final deportation orders, as deaths in custody climb and private prison giants GEO Group and CoreCivic rake in profits from ICE’s ballooning budget. Reichlin-Melnick explains how Trump’s mass deportation machine changed tactics after Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis and the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti – shifting to predawn raids, targeting people at airports and their own immigration check-ins, and quietly pushing arrests to 50,000 a month. Meanwhile, at least 60 people have died in ICE custody in Trump’s second term. Reichlin-Melnick says the real number is likely higher: ICE has stopped reporting deaths right after release, and cut inspections as it opens new facilities. Immigration is “a creature of Congress,” Reichlin-Melnick says, and what Congress gave ICE, it can take away. But with Trump’s veto looming, oversight may be lawmakers’ most powerful weapon. Will the new Democratic Congress rein it in? Watch full episodes of BT Live, join breakthroughnews.org as a member today! #breakthroughnews

articles.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 | Propaganda for US war in Korea?
articles.author: Amanda Yee
articles.content: The new Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 just dropped, and it’s already mired in controversy. The game simulates urban warfare in Seoul, casting players as a South Korean marine fighting off an invasion from the DPRK. Is this video game harmless entertainment, or is it sophisticated imperialist propaganda designed to “manufacture consent” for war against North Korea and normalize US militarism? Ju-Hyun Park, organizer with Nodutdol for Korean Community Development and director of engagement at Breakthrough News, joins Amanda Yee to break down the dangerous political messaging behind Modern Warfare 4.

articles.title: Congolese president signs referendum bill that could allow for a third-term
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) President Félix Tshisekedi has promulgated a controversial law establishing the conditions for holding referendums. Opposition parties, civil society groups and grassroots movements have previously said it could allow him to seek a third term. The signing follows more than five months of protests, court challenges, and street mobilization against the law. The promulgation was announced on national television late on Tuesday, November 10. “The President of the Republic, Félix-Antoine Tshisekedi Tshilombo, promulgated, on November 10, 2026, through an ordinance, the law setting the conditions for the organization of the referendum in the Democratic Republic of Congo,” state broadcaster RTNC reported. Roger Kalenga, Deputy Spokesperson for the Head of State, read excerpts of the new legislation on air: “Law No. 26/045 of November 9, 2026, establishing the conditions for organizing referendums in the DRC. … The National Assembly and the Senate have adopted, and the President of the Republic promulgates, the following law: Chapter One, Purpose and Scope. Article One: This law establishes the rules relating to the purpose, procedure, initiation, and convening of referendums, as well as related offenses.” The bill went through parliament, where Tshisekedi’s coalition holds a large majority, first passed it in June while opposition members stayed away. The Senate vote was 89 in favor, none against, with 20 senators not taking part. In July the Constitutional Court ruled the law constitutional, subject to interpretive reservations on thirteen provisions. On August 10, Tshisekedi sent the text back to parliament for a new deliberation, which re-adopted it in October. Read more: Push for referendum in DR Congo sparks protests over possible Tshisekedi third term The opposition opposes the referendum The law has met resistance at every stage. In May, the main opposition parties, formed Coalition Article 64 (C64) named after Article 64 of the constitution, which obliges every Congolese to oppose anyone who seizes power by force or exercises it in violation of the constitution. In mid-June, days before the Senate vote, opposition parties and civil society groups marched in Kinshasa against the bill. Police and security forces dispersed protesters with tear gas. Several people were injured. With opposition figures accusing the authorities of suppressing peaceful protest and violating citizens’ constitutional rights. Read more: Several arrested in protests against constitutional changes in DRC Protests rocked the country again on September 15, when C64 called a nationwide day of action. In Kinshasa, hundreds gathered before the march was disrupted by clashes with members of the Force du Progrès, a group affiliated with Tshisekedi’s UDPS party. Police fired tear gas and warning shots, and at least 10 people were arrested in Kinshasa. Constitutional limits and Tshisekedi’s third-term ambitions Tshisekedi, who first assumed office in January 2019 following the December 2018 elections, was re-elected in December 2023 for a second five-year term. Under the current constitution, his mandate is due to end in 2028. The current constitution limits the president to two five-year terms; However, the proposed constitutional changes have raised questions about whether a new constitution could be used to circumvent these protections. Tshisekedi has previously defended the possibility of constitutional reform and indicated his willingness to remain in office beyond 2028. In May 2026, he said he had not sought a third term but would accept one if the Congolese people wanted him to continue governing. The new referendum law therefore represents an important development in the dispute. Although it does not automatically remove presidential term limits or guarantee a third-term bid, it provides a legal framework for holding referendums on constitutional matters, including the adoption of a new Constitution. With the legislation now in force, opposition parties and civil society organisations face a renewed challenge in their campaign to defend the existing constitutional order.

articles.title: Keytruda was built on public science. Why does Merck own the rewards?
articles.author: David Franco
articles.content: Keytruda is often presented as the ultimate success story of modern pharmaceutical innovation. And in one sense, that is true. Few medicines have transformed oncology as profoundly as pembrolizumab. It has extended survival in melanoma, lung cancer, and many other malignancies, and it has helped turn immune checkpoint inhibition from a scientific hypothesis into a clinical reality. For many patients, it has meant years of life that previously had few options at all. But that is only one part of the story. The other part is far less comfortable. Keytruda is not just a breakthrough drug. It is also a striking example of how the contemporary pharmaceutical system works: publicly funded science lays the foundation, private firms take control of the resulting assets, monopoly rights determine pricing, and health systems are then forced to pay extraordinary sums to access medicines they helped make possible in the first place. This is what makes Keytruda so politically important. It is not merely a story about scientific success. It is a story about ownership, public subsidy, corporate strategy, and the growing gap between biomedical progress and equitable access. In that sense, Keytruda is not an exception. It is one of the clearest illustrations of the current system’s structural logic. The science was public before the profits were private The foundations of Keytruda were laid long before Merck turned it into a blockbuster. The crucial scientific breakthrough came with the discovery of PD-1 by Tasuku Honjo and colleagues at Kyoto University in the early 1990s. Over time , this work revealed that PD-1 was part of the immune checkpoint machinery that restrains T-cell activity. That insight fundamentally changed cancer immunology. It suggested that instead of attacking tumors directly, medicine could work by releasing the brakes on the immune system. Read more: Against the normalization of limited access to CAR-T cell therapies This was not the product of isolated corporate brilliance. It resulted from decades of publicly funded research. Government support in Japan sustained Honjo’s work. In the United States , public funding helped establish the wider domain of immune checkpoint research. University laboratories, academic medical centers, and publicly funded research infrastructures made the field possible long before pharmaceutical firms recognized its full commercial value. That matters because the myth of drug innovation frequently begins too late in the story. It starts at the clinical trial, the patent filing, or the approval announcement, rather than at where innovation usually begins: in publicly supported science, collective knowledge production, and institutions built for the public good. Keytruda emerged from that ecosystem. Without it, there would have been nothing for the industry to commercialize. The market did not automatically recognize Keytruda’s value Another revealing aspect of the Keytruda story is that the drug was nearly lost not because the science failed, but because corporate priorities shifted. The antibody that became pembrolizumab originated at Organon, initially in a program not even designed for oncology. Through mergers and acquisitions, it passed to Schering-Plough and then to Merck. During these periods, the program was deprioritized, sidelined, and reportedly nearly discarded altogether. This should give pause to anyone who assumes that private ownership naturally distributes resources to the most socially valuable innovations. Under a system driven by portfolio logic, mergers and stockholder expectations, even a future life-saving therapy can be neglected if it doesn’t fit immediate strategic calculations. Big Pharma greed keeps lifesaving drugs out of reach for millions in the Global South. Source: ITPC/Facebook Pembrolizumab survived not because the market perfectly understood its promise, but because a handful of committed scientists persisted and external developments forced management to reconsider. Once competing checkpoint therapies began to show promise, Merck moved rapidly. What had been treated as marginal suddenly became central. This is often celebrated as corporate agility. But it can just as easily be read as evidence of structural irrationality. A therapy that would go on to become the world’s top-selling drug was almost abandoned because the system is not designed to maximize public health. It is designed to manage financial risk and competitive advantage. From breakthrough to blockbuster Once Merck committed to pembrolizumab, it did so aggressively. The company rapidly expanded the clinical program , scaled up trials , employed biomarker strategies with considerable success, and leveraged regulatory mechanisms to accelerate approval. Scientifically and operationally, this phase proved impressive. It helped bring a major therapeutic advance to patients faster than would otherwise have been possible. That achievement should not be dismissed. It shows that large-scale clinical development, regulatory coordination, and manufacturing capacity remain essential parts of turning promising science into real treatments. The question is not whether these capacities are needed. The question is who controls them, whose interests they serve, and who reaps the rewards. Because once Keytruda succeeded, the rewards were immense. Read more: Patents, profits and squabbles for share in the pie – Moderna’s pandemic story By 2024, it had become the world’s top-selling medicine, generating nearly 29.5 billion USD in annual sales. That figure is astonishing not only because of its scale, but because it reveals how enormous the extractive potential of pharmaceutical monopolies can be when attached to a clinically transformative product. And yet, even this commercial success was built on a landscape formed by public input . The scientific foundations were public. Clinical trial ecosystems depended heavily on academic hospitals and publicly subsidized research environments. Regulatory acceleration came through public institutions. The risks were socialized at crucial stages, but the financial gains were overwhelmingly privatized. A medicine can be revolutionary and still be exclusionary The great paradox of Keytruda is that a drug capable of redefining cancer care can simultaneously remain not accessible to many of the people who need it. In the United States, treatment costs have exceeded 150,000 USD per patient per year. In Europe , health systems have had to negotiate rebates , confidential agreements , and special reimbursement arrangements to contain budgetary impact. Even wealthy countries struggle to absorb the costs of widespread access. For lower-income countries, the situation is far worse. There, access is often minimal, delayed, or effectively nonexistent. This is not a side issue. It is central to how we should evaluate medical innovation. Read more: Not Omicron but greed of capital threatens the world A therapy cannot be judged only by its efficacy in clinical trials or its scientific sophistication. We must also judge it by whether patients can actually receive it. A drug that exists in principle but remains unreachable in practice is not a complete public health success. Keytruda’s inclusion on the WHO Essential Medicines List should have been a powerful recognition of its importance . But that recognition also exposed a deeper contradiction. What does it mean for a medicine to be considered essential if it remains priced beyond the reach of most of the world? At that point, the designation risks becoming symbolic. A medicine can be clinically essential and commercially exclusionary at the same time. Under the present model, that contradiction is not accidental. It is built into the system. The real question is not whether industry matters, but on what terms Defenders of the status quo often respond with a familiar argument: without patents, high prices, and private investment, drugs like Keytruda would never have reached patients. The claim that large-scale development requires resources, coordination, and risk-bearing has some truth. But that does not settle the matter. It merely restates the rules of the current system as if they were laws of nature. They are not. Read more: When Brazilian health workers discovered Soviet healthcare The issue is not whether clinical development and manufacturing require serious investment. Of course they do. The issue is whether public institutions must always play a subordinate role: finance early discovery, de-risk innovation, build research infrastructure, and then step aside once commercialization begins. Why should taxpayers fund the science, support the research ecosystem, and absorb part of the development risk, only to lose all control over pricing, licensing, and access at the decisive moment? Why should a medicine built on public knowledge become a private asset governed by monopoly logic? And why should governments then pay again, at inflated prices, to buy back access for their own populations? These are not radical questions. They are the basic questions that any serious public-interest pharmaceutical policy must confront. Public Pharma is not a fantasy but a necessary direction This is where the idea of Public Pharma becomes more than a slogan. It becomes a practical and moral challenge to the current order . A Public Pharma approach would begin from a simple premise: if public institutions are central to the creation of breakthrough medicines, they should not relinquish stewardship when those medicines become commercially valuable. Public actors should have the capacity not only to fund discovery, but also to shape development, retain ownership stakes, set access conditions, and, where appropriate, support manufacturing and distribution. That would not mean excluding scientific collaboration or denying the complexity of drug development. It would mean changing the terms of engagement. Under such a model, the benefits of a drug like Keytruda could be organized differently. Public investment could come with enforceable conditions on affordability and licensing. Intellectual property could be structured to prevent extreme monopoly control over entire therapeutic pathways. Revenues could be reinvested into further research rather than extracted as shareholder value. Health systems could negotiate from a position of public stewardship rather than defensive purchasing. Most importantly, access would no longer be treated as an afterthought. A breakthrough for whom? Keytruda demonstrates what biomedical science can achieve at its best. It shows that diseases once regarded as almost uniformly fatal can be confronted in entirely new ways. That should be acknowledged without hesitation. But Keytruda also shows the limits of celebrating innovation while ignoring political economy. A medicine can be scientifically brilliant and socially unjust at the same time. It can save lives while still comprising a system that rations access through price. It can stand as proof of human inventiveness while also revealing how poorly that ingenuity is governed. That is why Keytruda should be remembered not only as a triumph of immuno-oncology. It should also be understood as a case study in the contradictions of pharmaceutical capitalism. The lesson is not that we need less innovation. The lesson is that we need a different system for governing it. The real measure of a medical breakthrough is not only whether it can be invented, patented, and sold at scale. It is whether we can make it available, sustainably and fairly, to all who need it. On that question, Keytruda remains not only a success story but an unfinished indictment. David Franco is a scientist and public health activist based in Belgium. In the People’s Health Movement, he focuses on the Public Pharma for Europe (PPfE) initiative. David holds a PhD in Pharmaceutical Sciences from the Free University of Brussels. People’s Health Dispatch is a monthly bulletin published by the People’s Health Movement and Peoples Dispatch . For more articles and subscription to People’s Health Dispatch, click here .

articles.title: “Paraguay Is in Dire Need of Change”: Senator on Bank Collapse & Political Crisis
articles.content: The collapse of Ueno Bank in Paraguay has plunged the country into crisis and led to the ouster of right-wing President Santiago Peña, a staunch ally of the Trump administration. At least 3 million people — nearly half of Paraguay’s population — lost access to their accounts on November 3 after regulators seized the insolvent bank amid allegations of widespread fraud. Peña, who had close ties to Ueno and appointed a former executive to lead Paraguay’s central bank, attempted to resign the presidency following the bank’s collapse. Lawmakers, however, rejected his resignation and impeached him instead, thereby stripping him of immunity from prosecution. He has since been placed under house arrest. For more on the bank collapse and its aftermath, Democracy Now! spoke with left-wing Senator Esperanza Martínez, who called for a broad “national pact” among various political parties to navigate the crisis and institute reforms. “Paraguay is in dire need of change,” she said.

articles.title: “Parasitic Technology”: Could Jensen Huang/Nvidia Scandal Prompt Rethink About AI?
articles.content: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including with an employee and a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence officials accuse of spying for Beijing. The company says Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO as the board searches for a permanent replacement. Nvidia’s computer chips are at the heart of the artificial intelligence boom, driving the company’s value above $4 trillion and making Huang one of the most influential business leaders in the world. His spectacular fall from the company he co-founded in 1993 comes as the U.S. stock market has become highly dependent on a handful of AI-related companies and amid intense competition between the United States and China over control of the technology, with access to Nvidia’s chips becoming a major point of contention between the two countries. Tech critic Paris Marx notes that the AI industry’s “circular financing,” in which companies are both clients and investors for one another, has created systemic risk. We also speak with Ramesh Srinivasan, director of the AI Futures Lab at UCLA , who says the “soap opera” of the Huang scandal has exposed “how precarious the governance of this AI truly is,” with only a handful of people and firms controlling “incredibly powerful technology that feeds off of all of us and the planet.”

articles.title: “It’s Just Barbarism”: Dr. Feroze Sidhwa Mourns Friend Killed in Israeli Hospital Strike in Gaza
articles.content: Israel’s latest bombing of Nasser Hospital in Gaza on Thursday killed six Palestinians, including surgeon Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira. He was featured in the recent documentary American Doctor , which follows international medical volunteers in Gaza’s battered hospitals as they work alongside Palestinian colleagues. Israel claimed, without providing evidence, that it targeted a senior Hamas militant in the hospital strike. Israel has repeatedly bombed medical facilities in Gaza since the start of the genocide in October 2023, even though such attacks are prohibited under international law. “It’s just barbarism. I don’t know why we’re supporting this,” says Dr. Feroze Sidhwa, one of the titular American doctors in the documentary, who demands accountability for Israel’s actions and a change in U.S. policy toward the country. “That’s an American-made bomb dropped by an American-made airplane burning American-supplied jet fuel.” Sidhwa also comments on the catastrophic flooding in Gaza that has swamped the temporary shelters of tens of thousands of displaced Palestinians as Israel continues to block the entry of shelter materials into the territory. As a result, “babies are going to die of hypothermia in Gaza for the fourth year in a row,” Sidhwa says.

articles.title: The Rule of Law Project: New Effort Launched to Probe Corruption & State Violence in U.S.
articles.content: As Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January, party leaders say they intend to hold Trump officials accountable with stepped-up hearings and investigations. The administration, however, has responded with threats to launch its own investigations into lawmakers for carrying out their oversight responsibilities. “The oversight function of Congress is well established by the founders. It’s a normal part of government. The separation of powers requires oversight,” says Brad Adams, co-founder of The Rule of Law Project, which seeks to provide outside accountability due to what he describes as the administration’s refusal to investigate “obvious cases of corruption.”

articles.title: DPRK throws cold water on Trump’s summit hopes
articles.author: Ju-Hyun Park
articles.content: For nearly two years, Trump has touted a possible summit with the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) as an imminent possibility. While Trump became the first US leader to meet with his DPRK counterpart in 2018, his attempts since 2020 to rekindle the relationship have faltered. Last week, Washington’s hopes for a summit hit another road block of its own making. On October 31, the FBI issued a statement accusing the DPRK of conducting a massive $6.34 billion cryptocurrency theft from Binance wallets, the built-in digital accounts for users to manage exchanges. After denying the accusation, Pyongyang issued a stern response that hinted a new stance towards Washington could be forming as a matter of policy. In a statement given on November 4, Kim Yo Jong, Workers’ Party of Korea director of general affairs, declared, “the continued hostile signal of the US to our state compels the DPRK to reconsider the US entity in various aspects.” No change in position has yet been declared, but the statement offered a clear sign Pyongyang’s patience is wearing thin. Kim continued, “It is our clear stand that we have no need to sit face to face with such unreliable and hostile persons who refuse to abandon their policy of confrontation while talking about dialogue.” While Kim did not rule out the possibility of dialogue, she clarified that “this is not surely equated with national interests for us,” adding, “In the present reality when new records are being set in the implementation of the US hostile policy toward the DPRK, it is natural that new records should be created in our reflective counteraction.” The “invariable hostile policy” Kim’s response must be placed in the context of Washington’s overall policy of aggression towards the DPRK, rather than solely as a reply to the FBI. In her own words, “We do not regard the ‘Binance’ hacking incident as any accidental and sudden case or isolated private scheme, but as an extension of Washington’s invariable hostile policy toward the DPRK.” The phrasing of WPK and DPRK officials is often a subject of curiosity and mockery in English language media. Consequently, the deliberate choices of wording in official communications, and their implications on policy, are often overlooked. The phrase “hostile policy” is a longstanding term used by the DPRK to describe the hybrid war prosecuted against it by Washington. Here, the basic facts of the Korean situation bear repeating: The US is still at war in Korea, since the armistice signed in 1953 was never converted into a lasting peace agreement. To this day, the US retains 80 bases and military installations in Korea, and fields over 28,000 permanently stationed troops. The DPRK is widely recognized as one of the most sanctioned countries on earth, having been under some form of US unilateral coercive measure since even before its official foundation in 1948. The US and Republic of Korea (ROK) conduct joint war exercises for hundreds of days out of the year on an annual basis. Since 2023, these drills have increasingly included the participation of Japan under the trilateral JAKUS “security cooperation” established that same year — realizing a long-held dream in Washington to unite Tokyo and Seoul under a common war-fighting structure. Washington’s “hostile policy” is at the heart of its present diplomatic standoff with Pyongyang. While the US has made numerous appeals for a return to dialogue since the failure of the Hanoi Summit in 2019, the DPRK has rebuffed these attempts due to the lack of change in Washington’s posture. As Kim reiterated in her November 4 statement, “We have already and repeatedly clarified that the US abandonment of its hostile policy toward the DPRK is a major premise and key to solving all problems, and in this context it is needless to say that the US recent act is a clearly retrogressive one.” The accusation of masterminding the Binance heist is not the only recent example of the US “hostile policy.” In her statement, Kim also referenced ongoing US-ROK war drills, such as the recently concluded Freedom Flag air drills and Iron Mace nuclear war exercises, the imposition of new sanctions that ostensibly target DPRK remote workers, and the publication of the State Department’s annual Trafficking in Persons (TIP) report, which listed the DPRK in its lowest category for the 24th consecutive year. The TIP report is often cited as justification for additional US sanctions. Korea: Trump’s second quagmire While stumbling through the politically disastrous war in Iran and the backlash to ICE’s crackdown on immigrants at home, the Trump administration has at times looked to Korea as a source for easier returns on its political capital. At times, Washington squeezes Seoul for tributes Trump can brandish as trophies – Seoul’s recent capitulation to dispatch military units near the Strait of Hormuz comes to mind. Yet the real prize, a new summit with Kim Jong Un, continues to elude him. This August, Trump claimed to have made direct contact with Kim, and told the press he hoped to meet with the DPRK leader this year. Kim Yo Jong’s comments have thrown cold water on that hope at a sensitive time. Trump is scheduled to arrive in Manila on November 16 for the ASEAN Summit, after which he will travel to Shenzen, China for the APEC Summit from Nov 18-19. Last year, Trump attempted to use the occasion of APEC to schedule a meeting with Kim Jong Un that never transpired. While not yet as politically costly as Iran, the Korean Peninsula has become Trump’s second quagmire. The situations bear some remarkable similarities. Faced with a smaller but nevertheless formidable opponent, the US finds itself unable to proceed either diplomatically or militarily for fear of the political costs. In both cases, Washington may hope to wait out its opponents, but time is not on its side. As US sanctions weaken with time, Trump has few tools available to ratchet up the pressure on Pyongyang. Resolution in Korea is still possible, but Trump must be willing to pay the price. The DPRK is determined to set the terms of future dialogue with the US, and its conditions are clear: negotiations will not happen at gunpoint. The US president – whether it be Trump or some replacement – who dismantles the “hostile policy” will be given the opportunity to redefine Washington’s relationship with Pyongyang on the basis of equality. This would provoke the wrath of the Beltway, but in time, stand out as a historical achievement. The trade-off seems fair enough, but political miserliness may win out in Washington. US prestige is in short supply these days. The same could be true for Pyongyang’s patience. Washington would do well to come to the table sooner than later, while an invitation is still available.

articles.title: Trump renews designation of Nicaragua as an ‘extraordinary threat’
articles.author: John Perry
articles.content: On November 3, President Trump signed an executive order declaring a “national emergency.” The “emergency” is due to “the unusual and extraordinary threat to the national security and foreign policy of the United States constituted by the situation in Nicaragua.” Supposedly, this emergency began in November 2018, has persisted for eight years and is expected to continue into 2027. The scale of the “threat” Here are some key figures by which to judge the scale of the “threat” posed by Nicaragua. First, some basics. The US population is nearly 50 times Nicaragua’s and its economy is 1,400 times bigger, with Nicaragua’s national income (GDP) only 0.07% that of the US. Second, a military comparison. Nicaragua has one of the smallest defense budgets in the Americas, devoting just 0.6% of its GDP ($116 million) to its military. The US, of course, has the world’s biggest “defense” budget at $954 billion or more than 3% of its GDP (see chart), and Trump wants to make it even bigger. Nicaragua deploys around 12,000 military personnel, under 1% of its northern neighbor’s 1.3 million. Third, its military has little or no offensive capability. Its principal duties include preventing drug trafficking, protecting borders, and conducting maritime patrols. The military also responds to emergencies such as hurricanes and earthquakes and protects the nation’s vital coffee harvest, of which the US is the biggest consumer. So, the notion that Nicaragua – 1,200 miles from the south Texas border – threatens US security is clearly absurd. What, then, is the basis of the so-called “emergency” and what has Washington done to stop it in the eight years since it began? US campaign against Nicaragua In Trump’s first term, he signed the original executive order after the US-inspired coup attempt against Nicaragua’s then recently re-elected Sandinista government in 2018. The anticipated collapse of the government in the face of a violent uprising failed to materialize. Trump’s executive order was an integral part of a political and media campaign to ostracize Nicaragua internationally. Bodies such as the UN’s Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) and the Organization of American States (OAS) were instrumentalized to attack Nicaragua’s human rights record, even though they had sent delegations to the country in 2018 that received evidence of assassinations and torture perpetrated by the coup-mongers. Washington started to put the squeeze on Nicaragua’s economy, cutting off access to loans from bodies such as the World Bank and the IMF, worth $500 million annually. Government officials were sanctioned, often on the basis of little or no evidence . Vital trade arrangements were threatened, including its membership in the regional free trade agreement that improves access to the US market. Media campaigns attempted to target Nicaraguan goods, such as its beef exports . Under Biden, the US Trade Representative launched a spurious investigation into Nicaragua’s allegedly unfair trade practices, such as use of child labor. Biden also launched a damaging “humanitarian parole” scheme designed to lure away skilled Nicaraguans, one reason for an increase in their migration northwards. Trump’s second administration imposed worldwide tariffs that singled out Nicaragua for higher penalties than its neighbors. Washington even attempted to damage Nicaragua’s important tourism sector by raising its travel advisory in 2018 to the same level as those for Guatemala and Honduras, where violent crime is much more prevalent. Nicaragua was refused help during the Covid pandemic. Consequently, its tourist trade recovered more slowly than in countries like Costa Rica. Visits by cruise liners, an important outlet for Nicaragua’s many artisan crafts, have never returned to previous numbers. Renewed executive order Despite these hostile measures, Nicaragua’s economy made a robust recovery after the damaging attempted coup of 2018 and the subsequent COVID-19 pandemic. In 2025, Nicaragua recorded the region’s fastest GDP growth, along with low public-sector debt and high foreign reserves. Its 2027 budget forecasts higher spending but a lower deficit. S&P Global Ratings has recently upgraded Nicaragua’s credit rating. Precisely because Nicaragua successfully fended off Washington’s attacks and rebounded, the hegemon was compelled to renew its proclamation of an “extraordinary threat.” According to Trump’s executive order, Nicaragua poses three main “threats” to US security and foreign policy. First was the “violent response by the Nicaraguan government to the protests beginning on 18 April 2018.” These supposedly peaceful protests led to well over 200 deaths, including those of 22 police officers, and caused at least $1 billion of direct economic damage. Arguably, Nicaragua’s defensive actions were much more measured than Washington’s would have been if confronted with similar violence. Second, Trump’s order hypocritically cites the “dismantling and undermining of democratic institutions and the rule of law” together with “indiscriminate violence and repressive tactics against civilians.” In fact, the measures taken by the Nicaraguan government to defend ordinary people and their constitutional rights have largely responded to US-funded criminal attacks and political interference. Third, Trump calls out alleged “government corruption” contributing to “economic destabilization.” Again, this grossly hypocritical charge hardly squares with Nicaragua’s economic achievements or its massive success in improving life for ordinary Nicaraguans. They have seen poverty reduced to under 14%, along with major improvements in public health services, free education, subsidized housing and infrastructure such as water supply, electricity, highways and public transport. The real threat The real strategic threat to the United States is Nicaragua’s ability to improve the lives of its citizens while maintaining a strong economy, despite Washington’s best efforts to prevent it. Trump’s renewal of the executive order signals that these threats will continue. His newly appointed chief of staff, Stephen Miller, identified Nicaragua as an exception to the realignment of countries behind Trump’s agenda for the hemisphere. He euphemistically suggested that the US could secure “a better future for the people of Nicaragua” via its regional alliance, the “Shield of the Americas.” All three of Nicaragua’s immediate neighbors are part of Trump’s “Shield.” Secretary of State Rubio has used the OAS to push Nicaragua into compliance. Although the country is no longer an OAS member, ten Latin American nations have been persuaded to participate. This arrangement could further threaten Nicaragua’s trade links, its diplomatic status and even regional air connections. The OAS is convening again on December 1 to decide how to ramp up this pressure. The ultimate hypocrisy in Trump’s executive order is, of course, that it is the US that poses an ever-present strategic threat to Nicaragua, not the other way around. Nicaragua-based writer John Perry is published in the London Review of Books, The Grayzone, CovertAction and elsewhere. Roger D. Harris is active with the Task Force on the Americas and the US Peace Council . Both are members of the Nicaragua Solidarity Coalition .

articles.title: Hegseth’s impeachment dodge, the draft, & the troops who won’t fight | w/ Mike Prysner
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth dodged impeachment this week thanks to 11 no-show Democrats on Hakeem Jeffries’ watch. Mike Prysner, Iraq War veteran and executive director of the Center on Conscience and War, joins Zoe Alexandra and Rania Khalek to unpack the charges in Rep. Thomas Massie’s articles of impeachment – from an illegal war on Iran that opened with the bombing of the Minab girls’ school, to a boat strike killing spree in the Caribbean and Pacific that has left more than 230 people dead. Opposition to war got Democrats elected, Prysner says, and at the first chance to deliver, “they just completely slept on it.” Prysner says conscientious objector filings are at a 25-year high, and they nearly all cite Minab. Not afraid for their own lives, he says; they refuse to hurt people they have no reason to hurt. He explains why a generation that grew up watching Gaza on their phones won’t fight in Trump’s wars, and why Hegseth’s Christian nationalist, anti-DEI overhaul of the military targeting women and Black soldiers is driving even more troops out. So starting next month, eligible young men will be automatically registered for the military draft. Prysner explains what automatic Selective Service registration really means – and how to prepare. Watch full episodes of BT Live, join breakthroughnews.org as a member today! #breakthroughnews ****** Rough transcript follows: [Speaker 1:] What is set to change on December 18th is that you will no longer have the choice to not register. You will be registered for the draft automatically by Grock or Palantir or whatever AI company. They’re going to scrape the data of Americans and put them on this draft list. It has a lot of problems. It puts you on a draft list when you don’t want to be, making you eligible to be drafted. Even being on the list should be a problem because the draft system was created as a show of force for the US to intimidate and threaten countries around the world. It was created during the Soviet intervention in Afghanistan, where the US was supporting Osama bin Laden. It was specifically a show of force in the Cold War. This week, the US House of Representatives failed to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, thanks to 11 Democrats who skipped the vote. This impeachment motion was brought forward by Republican Representative Thomas Massie from Kentucky. He raised charges around Hegseth’s conduct regarding the war on Iran and the deadly strikes on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific. This failure to impeach Hegseth has opened up a broader conversation about Democrats’ ability to carry forward these promises and what Hegseth has done as Secretary of War, what it has meant for the US military, and his attempts to deify the US military. To talk about these aspects and what it means, we are joined by Mike Prysner, a US Army veteran and the executive director of the Center on Conscience and War. Mike, thank you for joining us here at BT Live. [Speaker 2:] Thanks for having me. Again, on Tuesday, thank you to those 11 Democrats who, for some reason, just couldn’t be present for that vote. Great job, Hakeem Jeffries, just doing his job. It was the outgoing Republican Representative, Thomas Massie, who raised this impeachment of Pete Hegseth for his conduct in the Iran war and these boat strikes. Beyond this failure of the Democrats to carry this out, talk to us about these crimes. Why are the Pentagon’s actions in Iran and in the Caribbean and Pacific illegal? What are we talking about here? [Speaker 1:] It’s a violation of the War Powers Act, which has been going on for more than 60 days without congressional approval. Every administration in my lifetime has done this, especially in the war on terror era. It’s not abnormal, but the fact they are targeting Hegseth over this is significant. One of the main issues is the Minab school bombing, which has had resonance throughout the country and within the military. Of the more than 150 service members since the Iran war began who have filed as conscientious objectors, almost all mentioned the Minab school bombing as significant in their decision. For the administration, they want it to be something they gloss over, but it hasn’t gone away. We still receive calls from people for whom that was a turning point, leading them to take action to get out of the military. That being part of the articles of impeachment for Hegseth is important. His response to that was to hold a press conference saying he was proud of everything that happened and would do it again. The Pentagon’s investigation of the Minab school bombing claimed it was based on old intelligence, saying it was a military target when it wasn’t. It was a mistake on their part. Hegseth isn’t using the typical justification for war crimes. He’s saying he’s proud of it and would do it again, even as the war continues. The US is still launching strikes on Iran and Iranian forces around the world. So, the morning of his impeachment, he said this big war crime, which has caused so much revulsion in the country and the military, is something he would do again. Supposedly, we’re being promised that it’s not the end, and they will try again in January. But people of my generation have learned to have very low expectations. [Speaker 2:] Meanwhile, it’s incredibly frustrating because we’re in this doom loop. One day, there are back-channel negotiations, and Trump says the war is effectively over. Then, as we’re live streaming, Trump declares on Truth Social that the US no longer needs a deal with Iran, halting diplomatic efforts led by Vice President JD Vance. We’ve had you on several times since this war started in your capacity as executive director at the Center on Conscience and War. Your organization has been fielding hundreds of calls from active-duty service members seeking information about becoming conscientious objectors, especially during peak times when it seemed like the war would escalate into a ground invasion. Can you talk about that? I’m sure it ebbs and flows depending on how serious it seems like it’s going to escalate. And not just with Iran. You mentioned the Minab school bombing and the boat strikes, killing fishermen. The US has sent troops to Latin America to expand its military presence. The escalation of war with Iran across the region is intense. What are you hearing now? Are you still getting those kinds of phone calls? Does it go beyond just the Iran war? [Speaker 1:] Absolutely. Relating this back to Hegseth’s impeachment, the Iran war was a consequential factor in the midterm election. It handed the Democrats a historic victory, and the first chance they got to deliver on that issue with the impeachment vote, they completely slept on it. It sets the tone going forward. The fact that it was such a consequential issue in the election, even in deep red Trump states, shows it’s a unifying issue among Americans. People in the military aren’t immune from those sentiments. They come from the same communities that voted big in repudiation of the Iran war. We still get many calls and new clients who have come to this decision. We’re dealing with members of the military revolted by the boat strikes in Operation Southern Spear and Operation Epic Fury, and people directly involved in those operations. We’ve taken clients who were deployed in those operations on the ground in Latin America, part of the Venezuela raid that kidnapped Maduro, part of the boat strikes on the ground in Ecuador, and other places. People who were key in targeting operations have told their commanders they’re not doing this anymore. It’s a big trend that continues. It rivals the trend during the entire war on terror. It speaks to the generation of people in the military today. Most of our clients were born after the invasion of Iraq. They’ve grown up with the war on terror as a background. They’ve seen the disasters where people died for no reason. They were completing their training when the US withdrew from Afghanistan in total defeat, showing that 20 years of fighting was for nothing. They were completing training or entering their military units during the war on Gaza. Young people in the military today saw on their phones the impact of US weapons and policy on a population. That played a massive role in how they view conflicts they’re part of. When the Iran war started with Israel, a country they grew to hate by watching these things unfold on their phones, they realized they had a direct role. If they were morally opposed, they had to take measures to stop. It’s encouraging that we have this level of resistance when there isn’t an active ground war. The last thing I’ll say is it’s a level of resistance when Americans aren’t really getting hurt and dying. There have been deaths and injuries, but the people contacting us are rebelling not because they think something will happen to them, but because they don’t want to be part of hurting others they have no reason to hurt. [Speaker 2:] That’s an important point. I wanted to talk about the culture of the military under Hegseth or the attempt to ignite a cultural shift. We’ve seen these cringe videos posted on the Pentagon and the Secretary of War’s page of him working out at different bases and giving patriotic, nationalistic speeches. Hegseth has spearheaded efforts to root out DEI policies in the military while embracing a Christian nationalist, hyper-masculine culture. Can you talk about the motivation behind this cultural shift and how it has clashed with the growing consciousness among the military ranks? [Speaker 1:] One reason Hegseth is doing this is part of his campaigning for president in 2028, to be this culture war figure. He’s a true believer, coming from an extremist Christian nationalist, white nationalist tradition. His most prominent tattoos are crusader tattoos. He has a chapter in his book called “Make the Crusades Great Again,” advocating a holy war against Muslim countries. That culture has specific views of masculinity, and it’s been behind much of his work as Secretary of War. This isn’t playing well with the military as it exists today. Reporting shows that more than half of people in the military have decided to end their careers early because of Hegseth and the changes he’s making. It’s not playing well with those in the military, but that’s the point. Hegseth is getting rid of trans people in the military and purging black men through policies like the shaving profile. He’s cultivating a religious sector in the military, drawing in people who like his extremist ideology and getting out those who don’t. It’s dangerous because Hegseth wants to transform the military into something that reflects his ideology. What does that military look like? It’s a lot more dangerous and scary than the military today, which is less political than he wants. [Speaker 2:] Congress has made registration for the Selective Service automatic in the 2026 National Defense Authorization Act, signed by President Trump last December. Implementation is due by December 19th, but the agency withdrew its proposed rule in July and hasn’t said how it will meet the deadline. Can you tell us what automatic registration is? Why does it matter, and what does the push to make it automatic tell us about how the US is thinking about the future of war? [Speaker 1:] For over 40 years, since the Selective Service was created, if you are assigned male at birth, you are required by law to register yourself for the draft when you turn 18. But if you don’t, they don’t enforce it. Technically, you can go to prison, but they have never enforced it outside of the early 80s when people publicly refused to sign up. Since then, most young men don’t register, and nothing happens. If you’re not registered, you can’t be drafted. What is set to change on December 18th is that you will no longer have the choice to not register. You will be registered automatically by an AI system. It puts you on a draft list when you don’t want to be, making you eligible to be drafted. Being on the list is a violation of conscience for many, as it’s part of a show of force to intimidate countries. Reagan and Clinton called it a low-cost insurance policy to show the world millions of Americans are ready to be called up. The good thing is they haven’t introduced the regulations for public comment, so they shouldn’t be able to start registering people automatically on December 18th. The requirement for you to register yourself will lapse. But the Trump administration is not known for following the law, and they could start registering people using an AI system, violating the rights and conscience of many. There are things you can do to prepare. The Center on Conscience and War provides information on ways to preemptively plan to avoid being drafted. Being on the draft list itself is offensive to many. The US doesn’t want to use a draft, as learned in Vietnam, but that doesn’t mean they won’t use it. They don’t want to have to use a draft, but they want to be ready. The implementation of automatic draft registration is because self-registration wasn’t working for them. People didn’t want to be registered, so they didn’t sign up. It’s eerie, and in Germany, there’s a massive student movement against a mandatory draft. We’re seeing this trend worldwide, but also a lot of resistance. We’ll come back to you, Mike, in December to see how this plays out. Thank you for joining us on Breakthrough News Live to talk about Hegseth and all of his policies. [Speaker 1:] Thanks for having me.

articles.title: Israel resumes its lethal assaults on Gaza’s healthcare with new massacre at Nasser Medical complex
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: In yet another horrific assault on Palestinian healthcare system in Gaza and a major violation of the US-brokered “ceasefire” deal, Israeli warplanes struck Nasser Medical Complex in the southern city of Khan Younis on Thursday, November 12. The deadly airstrike, which hit the Al-Yassin surgery building at the complex, killed six people and injured dozens of others. Among the dead was a 13-year-old boy and a surgeon, Dr. Rizk Abu Shaaira. Dr. Abu Shaaira who appears in the recently-released documentary “American Doctor”. Nasser Medical Complex: a target for frequent Israeli assaults The massacre is not the first Israeli offensive on the facility, as the site has been targeted in multiple previous airstrikes since day one of Israel’s genocidal aggression on the Gaza Strip. On October 7, 2023, an Israeli airstrike targeted a Palestinian Red Crescent ambulance outside Nasser Medical Complex, leaving several casualties including a paramedic. On March 23, 2025, the surgical department of the hospital was struck, leaving five people killed. Less than two months later, the burns unit within the same surgical department was targeted by an Israeli drone. Palestinian journalist Hassan Islayeh and local police official Ahmed Al-Qudra were assassinated in the strike, while twelve other patients receiving medical treatment were wounded. On May 19, 2025, Israeli fighter jets hit a warehouse at Nasser Medical Complex, destroying 30% of the medical supplies stored there. Three months later, the Israeli air forces carried out a double-tap strike on the complex, killing 22 people. The fatalities included five journalists and four medical personnel. In addition to the repeated strikes, the renowned medical facility, which is deemed the largest hospital in southern Gaza, was raided and besieged between January and February 2024. At the time, Israeli forces had surrounded the compound for weeks, targeting it with heavy shelling and sniper fire that depleted vital supplies of fuel, food, and medicine. The Israeli military also forced thousands of displaced civilians to evacuate the facility, which was their only shelter during the coldest months of the year. Read more: Yet another catastrophic winter in Gaza Between March and April of the same year, Israeli forces renewed the siege on the hospital, which resulted in a complete operational shutdown. After the military withdrew from the facility, investigators discovered mass graves containing hundreds of bodies on the property. Israel uses same pretext, accuses Hamas of using facility as military headquarters Citing the same pretext it already used every time a medical facility in Gaza was struck, the Israeli military announced that it attacked Nasser Hospital on Thursday because Hamas allegedly converted its second floor into a military headquarters. The Israeli forces further claimed that the commander of Hamas’s Khan Younis Brigade, Mohammad Abu Ismail, and a number of the Palestinian group’s fighters were targeted in the airstrike. Hamas describes Israel’s claims as “repeated lies” to cover up a new war crime Hamas issued a statement refuting Israel’s allegations and describing them as “repeated lies” that aim to cover up the crime of targeting a medical facility. “The attacks on patients, doctors, and health workers disproves the occupation’s narrative and exposes its systematic targeting of the health sector in Gaza,” the statement asserted. Analysts viewed this escalation as an attempt by Israeli Caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to prove that he is more capable of “eradicating Hamas” than his rival, Gadi Eisenkot, especially as the latter is racing against time to form a new Israeli government – a race for which civilians in Gaza and other parts of the region would seemingly pay the price. Read more: Anti-Netanyahu bloc led by Eisenkot tasked with forming new Israeli government It is worth noting that Thursday saw the killing of a number of other people in separate Israeli attacks across different parts of the war-ravaged enclave, including Gaza City (particularly near the entrance of Al-Shifa Hospital), Deir al-Balah, Bureij , and Jabalia.

articles.title: Ex-partner of powerful far-right Latin American political operator receives asylum in Mexico
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: Several weeks ago, Latin America listened intently to the story of a Bolivian woman who had been shot on August 17 and, from a hospital, accused her ex-partner of ordering the hit job. Despite the sordid nature of the story, the news made the front pages of several news outlets because the person making the accusation was Nadia Beller, the ex-partner of Fernando Cerimedo. Cerimedo gained political notoriety in the region as one of the most influential political operatives of the far right in Latin America. Cerimedo was involved in several campaigns supporting far-right candidates who went on to become presidents: Jair Bolsonaro in Brazil, Javier Milei in Argentina, and Nasry Asfura in Honduras. In addition, he served as an advisor to President Rodrigo Paz in Bolivia, and his possible involvement in the campaign of the current Chilean President José Antonio Kast is under investigation. Cerimedo managed to become a highly effective operator not only because of his political communication advice and strategies, but also because he was linked to the operation bots farms and was one of the founder of the international right-wing news platform La Derecha Diario. Read more: Attempted murder accusations, troll farms, and presidential connections: the notorious case of Fernando Cerimedo Thus, the charges against Beller were not directed at just another far-right extremist, but at a very powerful individual with connections in the highest echelons of Latin American governments. Cerimedo was arrested by Bolivian police as he was attempting to leave the country by plane, just a few hours after the assassination attempt on August 18. The main reason for the arrest was the discovery of several messages on his cell phone which, according to the prosecution, link him to the perpetrators of the attack against Beller. Following this, Beller expanded on his account of the events and went so far as to accuse Cerimedo of being part of an operation to monitor flights transporting illicit narcotics and of having ties to the highest circles of power in Bolivia. She also stated that these and other accusations were putting her life at risk, which is why she sought asylum at the Mexican Embassy, where she was staying while her request was being processed. On Wednesday, it was reported that the Mexican government approved Beller’s request. For its part, the Bolivian Foreign Ministry reported that it had approved a safe-conduct pass for Beller, who traveled to Mexico on November 11. Apparently, the reason the process was expedited was due to Beller’s allegations that the police were preparing to arrest her for having released audio recordings linking Cerimedo to crimes. Among them are conversations that allegedly confirm Cerimedo’s involvement in appointing public officials, discussing the country’s public policies, and planning police operations. In response, Bolivian Minister of the Interior Marco Antonio Oviedo stated that although Beller has left the country, the investigation into the Cerimedo case (which currently includes four separate probes) will continue. For now, the question remains: will Beller, now safe in Mexico, disclose the rest of the information she claims to have regarding the ties between her ex-partner – a powerful political consultant – and the upper echelons of the Latin American far right?
